FinanceTab.title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
FinanceTab.text:
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.

Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.

McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."

The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.

Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.

McDonald's workers speak out over sexual abuse claims

McDonald's boss on abuse claims: 'I don't want to talk about the past'

Every McDonald's warned over staff sexual abuse

Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.

She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.

"I got the hell out of there," she says.

Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.

Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".

Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.

"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.

"And why would you? That is literally a child still."

Hundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.

The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.

The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.

Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.

Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees".

"It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it a lot safer, I think, as well. And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''

She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out.

"And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"

FinanceTab.title: Viagogo may have broken law on hidden fees, watchdog provisionally finds
FinanceTab.text:
Ticket-reselling site Viagogo may have broken the law on hidden fees, the UK's competition body has said in a provisional finding.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it found that Viagogo failed to show consumers the total price upfront when they were buying tickets "and added fees later in the process, a practice known as drip pricing".

The CMA added that this was an initial finding, and it should not be assumed that the company had actually broken the law.

In a statement, Viagogo said it was co-operating fully with the CMA, adding that the investigation was continuing and "no final findings have been made".

The CMA said last year that it was investigating a number of companies over their online pricing practices, including Viagogo.

The competition watchdog said it had looked into the experience of UK fans buying tickets for events such as concerts and sport on three websites that operate under the Viagogo brand.

"The CMA believes that mandatory costs such as taxes and booking fees were added at later stages of the checkout process and not included in the total price from the start," it said.

"Drip pricing can cause fans to be caught out by extra charges and buy tickets they might not otherwise have selected, had they been able to compare prices accurately from the start."

The CMA said Viagogo would now have an opportunity to consider its findings and respond before a final decision is made.

"This is an ongoing investigation and no final findings have been made," Viagogo said in a statement.

"We have engaged constructively with the CMA and continue to cooperate fully with its investigation."

The CMA has powers to tackle anti-competitive behaviour. It can now decide if consumer laws have been broken - rather than having to go through the courts.

Drip pricing is one of the practices the CMA has been focusing on particularly.

On Wednesday, it said it was investigating three companies, external over the issue, and in August it announced that the Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and RED Driving School had been engaged in the practice.

In general, the CMA can impose penalties of up to 10% of global turnover for a breach of consumer law. However, it will consider a number of factors, including the severity of conduct, before deciding on the size of the penalty.

In June this year, the watchdog ordered rival ticket reseller StubHub UK to refund more than 50,000 customers and pay a £900,000 fine for not showing people the total price upfront when buying tickets.

StubHub UK received a 40% reduction to its financial penalty after it admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early with the CMA.

FinanceTab.title: What is happening with the Scottish government's bonds?
FinanceTab.text:
The Scottish government is facing questions about its plan to issue its first ever bonds.

The move would allow ministers to borrow money from investors who in return receive regular interest payments.

The aim is to raise about £1.5bn by the end of the parliamentary term, with the funds to be used on long-term projects such as building hospitals or maintaining roads.

Named "kilts", a nod to UK government "gilts", the scheme has provoked much debate.

This week, MSPs on Holyrood's finance committee heard about the potential risks and rewards.

A bond is a financial tool used by a government to borrow money. They are sold with a promise for the buyer, or investor, to be paid back at the end of an agreed term.

The government will also make regular payments to the investor.

In the UK, a government bond is called a gilt. They are typically bought by financial institutions such as pension funds, insurance companies and commercial banks.

As a play on this term, the Scottish bonds have been nicknamed "kilts".

The Scottish government has said it expects the bonds to be issued within this financial year, subject to market conditions.

Former First Minister Humza Yousaf commissioned initial work in 2023 after advisers in the Scottish government's investor panel recommended making bonds available to the market as a means of raising Scotland's profile and attracting investment.

In November last year, the government announced that it had received an identical credit rating to the UK's score.

This was based on "prudent fiscal management" and the country's economic stability - though ministers were warned this could change if Scotland moved towards independence.

With market volatility due to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, some have questioned whether now is a good time to launch bonds.

But at Holyrood, David McMillan, professor in finance and accounting at the University of Stirling, told MSPs: "You can't wait for a perfect time because there's going to be no perfect time."

The government wants to raise £1.5bn through bonds by 2031, although that would only be a fraction of its near £70bn budget.

About four-fifths of the Scottish government's budget is used on resource spending, which goes towards day-to-day costs such as funding the NHS, benefits payments and paying salaries.

A smaller portion is made up of capital spending, typically used on long-term physical assets such as buildings and bridges, or maintaining roads or paths.

The Scottish government is unable to borrow for resource spending other than to correct forecasting errors.

However, for capital spending, it can borrow as much as £450m a year at 2023-24 levels up to a total cap of £3bn - to be uprated with inflation.

Adjusted for inflation, the government could borrow about £491m in the current financial year, with a total limit of about £3.3bn.

Economists have noted that Scottish bonds would be a more costly way of borrowing than existing routes provided by the UK government through the National Loans Fund.

It has been estimated, external that interest rates on "kilts" would be 0.3 percentage points above gilts, plus an additional £2m per bond in administrative costs.

The Scottish government has not released costings, citing market sensitivities, but has insisted, external issuing bonds would represent value for money relative to the costs of borrowing through the UK scheme.

Ministers argue that issuing bonds would be a good opportunity to market the country to investors, and would be helpful if Scotland became independent.

Dr Ben Cormier, a senior lecturer at the University of Strathclyde's department of government and public policy, told Holyrood's finance committee that while the Scottish bonds could cost marginally more than the UK scheme, they would "bring flexibility to public finances and debt management".

McMillan agreed with the plans "in principle", but warned they would lose "credibility" with investors if limited to five years.

Cormier warned that independence was the one thing "that could materially change the nature of risk associated with Scottish bonds".

Conservative MSP Liam Kerr said bonds could be more expensive than borrowing through the National Loans Fund and voiced concerns about a lack of transparency in the programme.

McMillan agreed there should be "full information" available, saying: "You've got to have a clear, full and frank conversation with the public."

FinanceTab.title: Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as UK inflation rate rises again
FinanceTab.text:
Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in a year.

A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, ahead of the official announcement next week.

Some households will get a £100 payment to help with the rising cost of living, a policy which was announced in the Budget.

Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices, official figures show.

Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the US-Israel war with Iran has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.

Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.

Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.

Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.

VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January.

But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: "Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power."

FinanceTab.title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
FinanceTab.text:
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.

Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.

The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.

Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.

The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.

But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.

But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.

Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.

The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.

While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.

Technology stocks have lost value in recent weeks following the US midterm elections. Democrats, who now control of both chambers of Congress, are expected to be tougher on AI regulation. Some Democrat candidates opposed the rapid build of data centres required to run AI.

But Anthropic went ahead with its market listing, despite the market volatility, because it needed to tap into additional funds, said Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton told the BBC. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more and so the time has come."

Broader anxieties about the AI industry remain.

Competition from low-cost rival models is growing.

Expensive computer chips, necessary for the industry to operate, are in short supply.

And the US Federal Reserve is concerned about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss interest rates, as well as the high concentration of AI exposure among a small number of firms.

With additional reporting by Rachel Clun

FinanceTab.title: Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
FinanceTab.text:
Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year.

Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone.

But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how.

That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%.

Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels.

Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights.

How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit.

The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support.

The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation, external, as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills.

While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%.

So why the difference?

It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full.

There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed.

Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then.

The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data.

But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices.

Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater.

Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few.

Food is, of course, a necessity.

If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people.

One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings.

The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February.

Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come.

To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure.

The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down.

The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention.

As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay.

That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances.

FinanceTab.title: British hacker who stole $11m jailed for six years in US
FinanceTab.text:
A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.

US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.

The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.

Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.

Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.

It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.

Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.

The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.

The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".

The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.

The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.

For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.

The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.

In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.

Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.

FinanceTab.title: Anthropic valued at $2tn as shares begin trading after record-breaking IPO – business live
FinanceTab.text:
Anthropic valued at $2tn as shares surge 34% as trading begins

NEWSFLASH: Anthropic’s shares have started trading, giving the AI pioneer a valuation of $2tn.

After more than two hours, Anthropic’s share have begun trading… at a price of $111.50 each.

That’s 34% more than the $83 at which the company sold its shares in today’s IPO.

That IPO valued Anthropic at $1.5tn, but now that the shares are actually trading, it’s market capitalisation is up to $2tn.

Here’s the clip of Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, issuing a warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence, saying it has “very real” but “avoidable” risks, shortly before the company rang the opening bell at Nasdaq.

Richard Partington and Kalyeena Makortoff

Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.

She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe.

“This calls for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies,” she said.

Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen, Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is for ever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.

AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.

“To put it simply: you snooze, you lose,” she added. “Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.”

Read the full report here:

Sameer Shariff, co-founder and CEO of English language education company Cambly, noticed a buzz of energy among Anthropic employees as they were leaving the company’s headquarters in San Francisco yesterday.

Over the past two years, a few employees have left his company to join Anthropic. He’s been thinking about them today.

“I’m happy for them. It’s a big day for the market and for AI,” Shariff said, while chatting with a friend at Joe and the Juice in downtown San Francisco on Thursday. So far, “Anthropic has been funded by all these investors with the inside scoop. But this is a test of how Wall Street responds … all of a sudden the general public has access to participate.”

Shariff said he’s curious how the next six to 12 months will go. “I’m a big fan,” he added.

As we await the close of market valuation of Anthropic at the end of its first day on the market, Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at US-based Walser Wealth Management, wrote: “Anthropic’s IPO is exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment, which has been depressed with all of the negativity in the AI complex over the past several weeks.”

Walser added: “It’s possible that Anthropic could see volatility and downside moves during the Jensen Huang Senate testimony after Thanksgiving, because that is likely to reignite AI fears.

“But if that happens, it could be a good entry point for investors who want to buy Anthropic.”

On a drizzly morning in downtown San Francisco after a massive storm the day before, the mood was sleepy in the Andytown coffee shop atop Salesforce Tower Park. When asked about Anthropic’s IPO today, one barista said “What’s that?” — a clue that not everyone in this tech hub is obsessed with AI.

Anthropic workers do frequent the coffee shop, but they hadn’t seen any today, her colleague said. One patron, smiled when asked if he worked at the maker of Claude. “No, but I wish I did,” he said.

Out on the street, foot traffic seemed lighter than normal, likely due to the weather. But still some tech workers trickled into their offices at 9:30 a.m.

“I wish I was in that building,” a Meta worker, who declined to give his name, said entering his downtown San Francisco office and gesturing to one of Anthropic’s offices across the street. His friends who work at Anthropic have “big plans for what to do with their newfound wads of cash,” he said. “Some people are planning to backpack Asia,” he said. But mostly, they plan to keep working and liquidate slowly, he added.

Updated at 14.27 EST

Anthropic’s market value could exceed that of Meta Platforms, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, and make it more valuable than Coca-Cola, IBM, Starbucks, Delta Air Lines and General Motors combined, AP reported.

At that size, Anthropic could quickly join indexes that track wide swaths of the stock market, which in turn could bring in even more investment.

The company expects up to 20% of its Class A shares in the IPO to go to what are called “retail investors.”

But as part of the IPO, Anthropic is creating a special class of stock for CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei and five other co-founders, giving them 50.1% of the voting power of all the company’s outstanding shares.

That means the founders as a group could overshadow every other shareholder and dictate issues put before all investors, like how to vote on a potential sale of the company.

“Roll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company.

From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees.

And, to be fair, it wasn’t nailed-on that the show would go so swimmingly. There was a late risk that investor sentiment towards the AI universe could be jinxed – or Jensened – by the soap opera at Nvidia. More generally, there was a worry that the AI bubble, if that’s what it is, could burst when somebody tried to unload too much stock on the stock market in one go.

Anthropic is losing substantial amounts of money, according to its investor prospectus. In the first half of 2026, the company reported losses of $104bn in the first nine months of 2026. Those costs will continue to grow as the firm works to secure more compute. The company spent about $18.8bn on AI infrastructure in the first nine months of 2026.

Updated at 13.36 EST

Anthropic’s IPO will influence how Wall Street feels about other AI companies

Anthropic has become the first frontier AI lab to be publicly listed, enjoying a premium on its share price as a result of beating OpenAI to market.

The startup’s performance will serve as a bellwether for the AI industry and influence investors’ appetite for the massive costs of developing advanced AI.

Evan Schlossman, a principal at Neostellar, a publicly traded venture capital firm, said that investors are looking at whether Anthropic’s growth rate is sustainable and offset some of the costs of developing the AI.

“You’ve seen an astronomical growth rate in terms of the top line,” said Evan Schlossman, a principal at Neostellar, a publicly traded venture capital firm. “The question investors are going to be looking at leading up to the IPO, and once it’s public, is what happens to that growth rate.”

Updated at 13.36 EST

Further to that, all the major US stock market indexes are down, after an early morning rally quickly evaporated.

As of a few minutes ago, the Nasdaq sank 0.8%, the S&P 500 0.99%, and the Dow Jones 1.49%, and Anthropic’s share was ticking around $98.

US stock indexes tumbled ⁠on Thursday after Anthropic’s ⁠blockbuster market ​debut did little to alleviate concerns over the AI trade.

“It has failed to rekindle enthusiasm for ​tech stocks. We wouldn’t read too much ‌into the expected initial ‘pop’ ‌in Anthropic’s share price as a stock’s early trading tends to be noisy,” ‌Joe Maher, market economist at Capital Economics in London, told Reuters. “But how it fares in the coming months will be a key litmus test for investors’ enthusiasm.”

The listing follows weeks of selling in chipmakers and cloud companies as investors fretted over stretched valuations, heavy spending on AI infrastructure and the fallout from the abrupt exit of Nvidia ‌CEO Jensen Huang.

In the last 45 minutes since opening, Anthropic shares dipped to a low of $95, before rebounding to just above $100, where it is now hovering.

Anthropic’s initial public offering left more than half of the institutional investors bidding for stock without any shares, Bloomberg (paywall) reports, citing people familiar with the matter.

Per the report: “Allocations of the shares were heavily skewed toward US-based investors, with a large proportion of orders coming in from outside the country getting no allocation, they said. About 1,200 institutional investors placed orders, some of the people said.”

“It’s typically quite hard to get served on US IPOs when you’re located in Europe, particularly in very sought after deals like this one,” Christophe Pouchoy, a technology fund manager at La Financiere de l’Echiquier, told Bloomberg.

double quotation markThe book-runners had to make choices due to the huge demand and the vast majority of European investors were given no allocation at all.

Updated at 12.34 EST

A 34% ‘pop’ for a newly floated stock is not terribly unusual.

And while it suggests Anthropic could have raised more money in its IPO (by selling its shares at a higher price), there are sometimes good reasons not to do that.

Underwriters often decide to price an IPO below value, to attract buyers and ensure strong demand.

Dr. Paulina Roszkowska, Lecturer in Finance at Bayes Business School in London, argues that Anthropic’s board was right to “leave something on the table for their new shareholders”, explaining:

double quotation mark“Resist the temptation to squeeze out the highest possible price. Should an AI correction take 20 or 30 per cent off the shares in 2026/2027, investors will be less forgiving if management sold them perfection.

“After all, they may well need these investors again. With heavy losses and enormous spending plans, today’s generous valuation could become tomorrow’s fundraising problem. Investors remember who left something on the table and who took the table too.

FinanceTab.title: Labor leaders call on governments to stop awarding Amazon public contracts
FinanceTab.text:
More than 30 labor union leaders from 19 countries are calling on governments to review their public contracts with Amazon and Amazon Web Services, citing the company’s poor record on worker rights and collective bargaining, in an open letter published on Thursday.

“Amazon’s consistent record of disrespect for workers’ fundamental rights should disqualify it from being awarded public contracts – its behaviour is fundamentally inconsistent with the shared democratic values of our countries,” the union leaders wrote.

The letter cites Amazon’s anti-union activity around the world, including over a decade of strikes by workers in Germany, its decision to shut down its Quebec warehouses after a warehouse voted to unionize in 2024, allegations of retaliating and silencing workers in Australia and legally challenging labor laws in the US and Canada.

In the US, the Institute for Local Self Reliance estimates cities, counties and school districts spent $2.2bn on Amazon in 2023.

Amazon has also secured several multibillion-dollar contracts with the US federal government in recent years, including a nearly $2.6bn award from the Department of Homeland Security in 2026 and a 10-year contract with the National Security Agency that was renewed in 2022, reportedly worth up to $10bn.

“Our governments continue to award Amazon billions in public contracts for cloud computing services underpinning critical public infrastructure,” the leaders wrote. “This pattern reveals a dangerous disconnect between public procurement practices and the democratic values our societies are meant to uphold, while creating unnecessary risks for public services.”

Signers from the US include Stuart Appelbaum, president of the Retail Wholesale Department Store Union (RWDSU); Milton Jones, international president of the United Food and Commercial Workers; Claude Cummings Jr, president of Communications Workers of America; Sean O’Brien, president of the Teamsters; April Verrett, president of the Service Employees International Union (SEIU); and Jonathan Smith, president of the American Postal Workers Union.

Christy Hoffman, general secretary of UNI Global Union; Lana Payne, national president of Canadian trade union Unifor; Gary Smith, general secretary of the UK’s GMB; and Frank Werneke, president of ver.di in Germany also signed the letter.

“Every public contract is a choice about what governments are willing to pay for. Right now, taxpayers in country after country are paying Amazon while it shuts down warehouses, busts unions and tries to get labour laws struck down,” Hoffman said in a statement. “Governments set the rules for who gets public money. They can require that companies respect workers’ right to organize and bargain, and they should start with the biggest contractor that refuses to.”

The letter comes as the UK Home Office is planning to renew its Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud computing contract for a possible cost of £881.6m over two years.

Governments could reform public procurement rules to make certain worker rights standards mandatory for contractors along with establishing enforcement mechanisms that would exclude corporations that violate workers’ rights from future public contracts.

“Public funds should advance public values, not subsidize union busting or deepen our digital dependency on unaccountable corporate power,” the letter concludes.

A spokesperson for Amazon disputed the letter.

“This group is being intentionally misleading and continues to promote a false narrative. The fact is at Amazon we provide great pay, great benefits, and great opportunities – all from day one,” the spokesperson said in an email. “We directly employ more than 1.5 million people around the world, and provide a modern, safe, and engaging workplace whether you work in an office or at one of our operations buildings.”

FinanceTab.title: US ⁠judge allows Trump’s $15bn lawsuit against New York Times to proceed
FinanceTab.text:
A federal ⁠judge in Florida on Thursday said Donald Trump’s $15bn defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and book publisher Penguin Random House may proceed, a victory ⁠for the US president in his ⁠legal campaign ​against media companies he accuses of treating him unfairly.

US district judge Steven Merryday in Tampa dismissed two claims in the suit while allowing core defamation claims to move forward.

The president’s claim against the publishers alleges defamation by three New York Times reporters – Susanne Craig, Russ Buettner and Peter Baker – in two articles published by the outlet and a 2024 book Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father’s Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success, which was co-authored by Craig and Buettner.

Trump claims the articles and book contain false statements that damaged his businesses and personal reputation. An earlier, 80-page version of the complaint was thrown out because it did not contain a concise summary and was filled with “vituperation and invective”, the court said.

An amended, 40-page complaint was filed in October last year that removed references to the 2024 presidential election. Mediation talks failed, along with a request by the defendants to move the action to federal court in New York.

The Times and Penguin have denied defaming Trump and said in a court filing that his case is legally flawed and aimed at scoring political points.

In dismissing two of Trump’s claims, Merryday, an appointee of George HW Bush, said the rest of his complaint plausibly alleged that statements accusing ​Trump of “planning and perpetrating complex crimes” were “based on incomplete, minimal information.”

In his claim, Trump cited 22 statements from a ⁠book by Baker and 12 from the articles ​by Craig and Buettner. They include assertions about Trump’s role in ​creating his hit reality ‌TV show The Apprentice, ​his inheritance from ​his father, his business ventures and upbringing in New York City.

Representatives for the New York Times and Penguin Random House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesperson for the Times, has previously said “the lawsuit remains obviously meritless”. A spokesperson for Penguin Random House has also described the action as “meritless” and said it “stands by the book and its authors”.

Reuters contributed reporting

FinanceTab.title: Democrats demand answers from Howard Lutnick about Nvidia and his family’s business
FinanceTab.text:
The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, faces mounting questions over his handling of the Nvidia affair as Democratic lawmakers demand answers over his family firm’s vast stake in the tech company.

Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm Lutnick ran for decades before joining the Trump administration, held shares in Nvidia worth “hundreds of millions of dollars” while Lutnick made key decisions affecting the tech firm’s ability to operate, according to Democrats on three key congressional committees.

“The American people deserve to know: did the secretary of commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise US national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” said Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California.

Cantor Fitzgerald insists it had “no role” in the Trump administration’s decisions about Nvidia.

But in a letter on Tuesday to Lutnick’s son Brandon, who now serves as chair of Cantor Fitzgerald, the trio of lawmakers demanded documents and records, including communications concerning Nvidia.

They said that they wanted to “understand whether any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”.

Raskin is the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives. Meeks is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs committee. Kamlager-Dove is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs subcommittee on south and central Asia.

In an accompanying news release, the lawmakers said that they were seeking to determine whether Lutnick “blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China while his family’s firm held hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia stock”.

Howard Lutnick led Cantor Fitzgerald until his confirmation as commerce secretary in February 2025, when he transferred his stake in the firm to trusts benefiting his adult children.

In the letter to Brandon Lutnick, the lawmakers wrote that at the time of Howard Lutnick’s confirmation, Cantor Fitzgerald had “amassed a significant stake” in Nvidia, reportedly “holding more than 3.5m shares, valued at over $1.3bn”.

In a statement to the Guardian, a Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson said that the claims in the letter were “inaccurate”. “Cantor holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia,” the spokesperson said. “Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients.

“The decline in our holdings since early 2025 reflects the unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced their swap positions, not a Cantor decision to exit a proprietary position,” the statement continued. “Allegations suggesting that work influenced government decisions are baseless. Additionally, Cantor has no role in US export control or entity list decisions [to determine trade restrictions].”

The Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson also said that they were “confident that a full review of the facts will demonstrate that we have operated our business ethically and in full compliance with all applicable rules and regulations”.

In their letter, the lawmakers also cited a recent New York Times report that Howard Lutnick had pushed to weaken rules affecting south-east Asian datacenters, some of which are Cantor Fitzgerald clients.

A commerce department spokesperson told the Times that Lutnick makes policy decisions based on the best interests of the US and that he does not discuss department matters with his sons. The spokesperson added that Lutnick’s sons also do not discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him.

In their letter on Tuesday, the lawmakers asked Cantor Fitzgerald to provide written confirmation that it had “implemented appropriate preservation measures and instructed all relevant personnel to retain potentially responsive records” by 5pm ET on 1 December.

The letter comes after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, following reports of his multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The developments have put Lutnick into focus as last week Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, blamed Lutnick’s commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China.

SportsTab.title: England: Football Association punished by Uefa after fans' anti-Catholic chants against Spain in Nations League
SportsTab.text:
England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.

European football's governing body have fined the Football Association £12,572 (15,000 euros) and imposed a suspended one-match ban for England away supporters.

BBC Sport understands the charge of 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour' relates to chants that were deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish.

A further offence within the next two years would mean a ban on away fans is enforced.

There had been concerns of the prospect of racist chanting from Spain fans before the game in Madrid with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.

Tuchel stressed he didn't expect any incidents, but the visit was England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.

That led to a firm response from Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

England won the match 3-2 to end Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and top League A Group 3.

SportsTab.title: Mauricio Pochettino: Man Utd boss priorities include Fernandes, culture and defence
SportsTab.text:
"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."

Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.

The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.

He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.

The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.

Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.

So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?

There is a clear non-negotiable.

"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.

It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.

Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.

United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.

One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.

"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.

"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.

"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."

That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.

Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?

The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.

Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.

Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.

Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.

Then there is Dalot.

The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.

It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.

However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.

Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.

Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.

The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.

He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.

For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.

There is one issue Pochettino mentioned in his interview he will soon discover requires delicate handling.

United's match-going fans have stood by every manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired. There is no reason to think that will change now.

However, their relationship with the club's ownership is fractured, possibly beyond repair. Fresh accounts to 30 September show the club's overall debt remains more than £1.1bn and a further £14.5m was spent on finance costs in the previous quarter.

This fuels discontent in the stands, already heightened because of various ticketing measures, none of which are viewed by most supporters as being positive.

"We need to be united," said Pochettino.

"Chemistry is really important, chemistry between us and the staff and the fans and the players, the directors, the owners and everything."

SportsTab.title: Mauricio Pochettino: New manager's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
SportsTab.text:
Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.

Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.

Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.

"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator.

"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.

"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."

The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.

Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."

Manchester United have declined to comment.

SportsTab.title: Sandpapergate: Pat Cummins' Australia captaincy at a crossroads - Agnew
SportsTab.text:
Australia captain Pat Cummins, much like his fellow bowlers, is in the eye of the sandpapergate storm at the moment.

The reason is simple to me. The very notion that Cameron Bancroft - the most inexperienced batsman in the Australia team at the time – would use sandpaper on the ball against South Africa without the bowlers knowing has never made sense.

It has never seemed remotely plausible to me, as a former bowler, that the bowlers didn't know what was happening in Cape Town in 2018. It just doesn't seem possible.

Therefore, this day of reckoning was always going to come.

Let's be clear - as long as there has been cricket, there has been ball-tampering. There is no point hiding from the fact.

Back in the day it was about shining the ball, maybe using something like a sweet to get a sheen on one side.

Reverse swing was a ball-tampering game-changer. There was a requirement for a wearing process, roughing up and drying the ball.

But, to get one thing straight, whether a ball is being tampered with or not, it belongs to the bowlers. It is the bowling attack's weapon. As much as a bowler would not fiddle with a batsman's bat – sanding an edge or changing the grip - a batsman would not work on the ball without the knowledge of a bowler.

Some might wonder why revelations relating to the sandpaper controversy have not come to light before.

In response to that, I would say it would have been very difficult for a player in the Australia team to go public at the time. They would have been worried about their own futures, their careers.

Only when a player has retired, or believe their time as an international cricketer has come to an end, do they feel more comfortable to speak up.

I have also seen suggestions that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner have had their guilt diminished by what has emerged in recent days, that they took bullets for their team-mates.

Smith was captain and should have been in control of his team. Warner cooked up the sandpaper idea. Bancroft executed it. If they did take bullets, they were bullets they deserved.

Now, the spotlight has fallen on Pat Cummins, whose agent has repeated his client's version of events in the last 24 hours.

The junior bowler at the time, Cummins has ascended to the captaincy, often joked to be the second-most important job in Australia, behind only the prime minister.

Cummins is not a typical Australian captain. He is not abrasive, or in your face. When he says he has worked hard to correct the image of his team, he is credible. Then again, he missed a trick to really prove Australia are no longer a win-at-all-costs outfit with the Jonny Bairstow stumping in the 2023 Ashes Test at Lord's.

After everything he said in public, and the way he has been backed by Cricket Australia (CA), there seems to be no obvious suggestion Cummins has considered resigning, or that he will be sacked.

He is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on 9 December.

Looking ahead to that match, it is difficult to see how the build-up will be anything other than a circus, dominated by questions about sandpaper, who knew what and who said what to whom.

The litmus test for Cummins will be the public reaction. Remember, that Test is being played in Bancroft's home city, in the state of the newspaper where his 4,000-word testimony was first published.

If Cummins is still in his position by then, the response of the Perth crowd to the captain will be very interesting.

Even if Cummins does get through that, the Australian media will not let up. This is a huge story, one of the biggest in the history of Australia sport. The press will bang away until they feel they have got the truth.

And what about next summer's Ashes? If Cummins is tossing the coin at Trent Bridge on 18 June, then he is extraordinarily resilient.

Right now, I can't imagine that happening. He has said he never wants to talk about sandpaper again, which is ludicrous when you think what he will face on that tour: scrutiny from the media, constant baiting from the crowds.

Cummins will have to decide if he has the stomach for all of that, and whether he can see it through.

His way out could be to resign, without admitting guilt. To say the speculation has become a distraction for the team and the pressure is taking a toll on his family life – we have seen more pictures from Australia overnight of Cummins being confronted outside his home.

Cummins could perhaps continue in the ranks, just as Warner and Smith did. A resignation without an admission of guilt may also take the heat off the other bowlers – Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon.

Whether Cummins continues or not, questions will remain for others who were in Cape Town, Cricket Australia and the whole culture of the sport in that country.

Looking now at what happened in 2018, it appears there was an attitude in the Australia camp that they were fireproof, that they could get away with anything.

Credit goes to their media manager Kate Hutchison, who, according to Bancroft, made a stand about what was going on and knew what would happen if and when the Aussies got caught.

What about the others involved, coaches who were supposed to guide and protect young men? Darren Lehmann and his position at Northamptonshire, or David Saker, who has recently been working with England.

Cricket Australia has seemed so reluctant to get involved. If the big idea was to give individuals the opportunity to "tell their truth" behind closed doors, it is surely dead in the water.

What about telling THE truth? Nothing else is good enough.

SportsTab.title: Manchester City charges: Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if sponsors sue
SportsTab.text:
Premier League clubs have voted to cover legal expenses for the organisation's five board directors if any of Manchester City's sponsors sue them.

The clubs met in London on Thursday for the first time since City were found guilty of a catalogue of charges relating to the breaching of financial rules by an independent commission in September.

City have appealed and maintain their innocence, with a sanction yet to be decided.

The club's sponsors Etihad and Etisalat have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League.

At present, under the league's articles of association, a director is only financially covered should they win a legal case brought against them by a third party. But the league's rules will now be updated to extend legal indemnity for CEO Richard Masters, chair Alison Brittan and three other non-executive directors.

City and Nottingham Forest were the only two clubs that voted against the proposal to provide extra legal protection, with the other 18 clubs voting in favour.

Due to collective responsibility, it means that all clubs are now liable to cover legal costs that could run into hundreds of millions of pounds, raising the intriguing possibility of City being financially impacted by the legal action of its own sponsors.

It is understood City's CFO Ingo Bank asked Premier League chair Brittan during Thursday's meeting if the proposal was a direct result of threats of legal action from Etihad and Etisalat, but she said she could not comment.

While Forest have declined to comment, their objection to the proposal is said have to been on procedural grounds, rather than due to any support for City.

The club did not believe that sufficient information had been provided, or adequate time afforded, for clubs to properly consider the implications of the proposed amendment, particularly given the potentially significant financial responsibilities involved. It felt that such a decision warranted more scrutiny and informed consideration before clubs were asked to vote.

An independent commission appointed by the Premier League found City guilty of artificially inflating the club's revenues by over £830m over a nine-year period in September.

The commission determined that the club arranged "sham" contracts with sponsors, which disguised funding from club owners the Abu Dhabi United Group.

Premier League CEO Masters said City "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade".

In October, City sponsor Etihad Airways said it was considering legal action against the Premier League.

In a statement, the United Arab Emirates-based airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

Etisalat signalled its intention to follow suit earlier this month and described the Premier League's verdict as "entirely false and defamatory".

SportsTab.title: England vs New Zealand: George Furbank and Ollie Chessum back
SportsTab.text:
England have been boosted by the recovery and return of George Furbank, Seb Atkinson and Ollie Chessum to their starting line-up to face New Zealand on Saturday in the Nations Championship.

The trio, who all missed last weekend's win over Japan with knocks, are joined in the starting line-up by Will Joseph, who crossed for five tries against the Brave Blossoms.

Furbank held off the challenge of Freddie Steward, who impressed against Japan, to regain the full-back slot, while vice-captain Chessum brings ballast to a back row that is completed by Ben Curry and Ben Earl.

Fin Smith returns at fly-half to reprise a 10-12 combination with Atkinson that has started six of England's last seven Tests and dates back to their days as teenagers in Worcester Warriors academy.

Barring Joseph's inclusion for the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, England have named the same matchday 23 which combined excellently in the 45-12 victory over Australia a fortnight ago.

After last year's 33-19 success, England are aiming for successive wins over the All Blacks for the first time since beating them in November 2002 and June 2003 - five months before Rugby World Cup glory in Australia.

"There are few bigger occasions in international rugby than facing New Zealand," said head coach Steve Borthwick.

"It's a fixture that always carries a special significance, and one that the players are hugely looking forward to.

"We know the quality New Zealand have in their team. We've prepared for the very best version of them, knowing the challenge they will bring and the level we'll need to reach to get the result we want."

New Zealand, meanwhile, have also been bolstered by the return of big names.

SportsTab.title: Ireland v South Africa: Hosts name Dan Sheehan at number eight for Nations Championship match
SportsTab.text:
Ireland captain Dan Sheehan has been named at number eight for Saturday's highly anticipated Nations Championship match against world champions South Africa in Dublin.

Having won all 42 of his previous caps at hooker, the 28-year-old returns after recovering from a concussion to partner flankers Ryan Baird and Josh van der Flier in the back row.

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell has faced an injury crisis at number eight with regular skipper Caelan Doris, Jack Conan, Sean Jansen and recent debutant James McNabney all ruled out.

Nick Timoney, who was handed the jersey for last week's victory over Fiji, drops to the bench.

With Doris and Conan unavailable, Sheehan anchored the scrum in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster last month, but Saturday will be his first Test run-out in the back row.

"Most people would agree that he [Sheehan]'s a world-class player, not just good," said Farrell, who did not wish to comment on South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus' six-match ban for questioning the integrity of match officials.

"Throwing the ball in or scrummaging, his point of difference is in and around the field and how he plays the game with ball in hand or defensively, running lines and all of that.

"That's suited to number eight. He was training there all last week because he was on the 12-day return-to-play protocols, so we had a bit of a head start there, and he played there recently.

"He's very cool, calm and collected; there's no arrogance there whatsoever. Things don't bother him, so he takes it all in his stride, fully confident in his own ability."

Sheehan's move means that Ronan Kelleher keeps his place at hooker after starting the Fiji game, again joining props Andrew Porter and Tadhg Furlong in the front row.

After being rested last week, Joe McCarthy returns to the second row to partner Tadhg Beirne, with Van der Flier edging out Timoney for the number seven jersey.

Sam Prendergast starts at fly-half after being cleared to face the Springboks on Wednesday, with Jamison Gibson-Park retained at scrum-half.

Prendergast, 23, was cited for his hip-drop tackle on Fiji's Peceli Yato - which was not punished on the pitch - but an independent disciplinary panel ruled the challenge was not worthy of a red card.

"Nothing's changed for us all week," Farrell said when asked about the possibility of a Prendergast ban.

"There's always something going on, whether it's dealing with HIA (head injury assessment) injuries or incidents like we've had with Sam this week.

"It (the hearing) was late on Tuesday night; we trained Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday and Sam's done all of that so there's been no hiccups for us, let's say that."

Robbie Henshaw and Stuart McCloskey both return to midfield after Farrell opted to pair Jamie Osborne and Bundee Aki in a new-look centre partnership against Fiji.

However, Osborne was replaced by McCloskey in the third minute after sustaining a pectoral injury that has ruled him out of the South Africa game, while Aki drops to the bench.

With Hugo Keenan returning to full-back for his 50th cap after sitting out the Fiji game, Mack Hansen switches to the left wing with Robert Baloucoune retained on the right. Tommy O'Brien, who scored two tries from the left wing against Fiji, drops out of the squad.

Farrell has opted for a split of five forwards and three backs on the bench. Tom Stewart, Tom O'Toole, Sam Illo, James Ryan and Timoney provide pack cover with Craig Casey, Ciaran Frawley and Aki named as backline reinforcements.

SportsTab.title: Golf: LIV paid players millions as UK businesses owed thousands
SportsTab.text:
LIV Golf - backed by more than $5bn (£3.8bn) from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund - paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while leaving a trail of unpaid bills from UK suppliers.

BBC Sport has seen invoices from five small businesses totalling hundreds of thousands of pounds, all of which were overdue before LIV made its final payments to players.

Global Infusion Group,, external a Buckinghamshire company that provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event, is still owed £321,671, due on 7 August.

Suffolk-based BD365 Clean, external provided 108 cleaning staff and is owed £75,225, most of which was due on 20 July and 13 August.

"It just feels completely immoral," said Bonnie May, chief executive of Global Infusion Group.

"It really matters to a business of our scale. The impact has been huge, both personally and professionally."

Only $2m (£1.5m) has been earmarked so far by the Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure if they will receive anything at all.

Yet court filings reveal LIV made 59 payments to golfers on 31 July, amounting to $16.6m (£12.6m) and matching prize money for the same LIV Golf UK event.

A further $34.2m (£25.9m) went to players between 17 August and 3 September following tournaments in New York and Indianapolis, including $6.4m (£4.9m) to 2026 champion Jon Rahm just five days before the bankruptcy filing.

Four senior LIV executives also received retention bonuses totalling nearly $3m (£2.3m) in August.

"It's sickening," said Krissi Foskett, owner of BD365 Clean, who described the unpaid bills as "almost an extinction-level event" for her team.

"How can they sleep at night, knowing they are potentially putting companies out of business?"

Meanwhile, public records list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere,, external a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.

LIV Golf did not respond to our request for comment.

However, in August, LIV chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped they would be able to pay their suppliers.

"What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed."

The controversial breakaway league had been owned and bankrolled by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) since its launch season in 2022.

But in April, the fund announced it would end its backing after the 2026 season, putting LIV's future in doubt.

"Our understanding was that the funding would take LIV through 2026," said Global Infusion Group's May, whose company had about 60 staff catering for players and broadcasters.

"We weren't aware the funding had already stopped and there wasn't enough to actually fulfil their obligations."

PIF's multi-billion-dollar investment helped it to lure some of golf's biggest names and disrupt the PGA Tour's dominance of the sport.

"It's Saudi money, that's safe as houses, we thought," said Foskett.

"Their head honchos came along and enjoyed hospitality. We were there cleaning up at one o'clock in the morning then back in at five in the morning, only to be treated like this."

PIF remains the majority owner of Newcastle United, while Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 Fifa World Cup.

"I'm sure the country won't want to be saddled with the characterisation that it doesn't pay its bills," said professor Simon Chadwick, who is an expert in the business and politics of sport across Africa, Europe and Asia.

"I do find it surprising that they would simply walk away. I think they would want to engage in some kind of remedial action, particularly in terms of managing their image and reputation."

Filmmaker Joe Bentley spent eight days from April working on a video for LIV's YouTube channel that is still online.

He is owed nearly £6,000, with £2,226 due on 31 July.

The video was part of the 'LIV Back' series, set up to "focus on the impact LIV players and teams are making off the course".

He filmed at two schools taking part in 'Little Sticks', a LIV outreach programme which aimed to provide golf equipment and training in areas of deprivation.

"You feel massively deflated, a bit cheated and undervalued," said Bentley.

"Everyone I dealt with at LIV was lovely. The first email I sent chasing was to a production coordinator or a manager and even she was appalled that we hadn't been paid."

Gateshead Council is also owed £1,912, due on 22 August, relating to 'Little Sticks'.

"Transformation is not a short-term process," said Professor Chadwick.

"If you're going to embark on investment programmes in community sport, grassroots sport, you've got to make a long-term commitment and those changes have got to take place."

Fourteen golfers were among the published creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims.

Rahm topped the list with a claim of $7.5m (£5.7m), which he agreed to give up as part of his deal to leave the league.

Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m/£4.3m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m/£4.2m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m/£3.6m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m/£2.6m) also featured.

IMG Media, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and British golf YouTuber Rick Shiels were each listed with claims of more than $1m (£760,000) too.

Meanwhile, BBC Sport understands the R&A is owed about £500,000 for advice on sustainable maintenance of courses used by LIV.

A hearing is scheduled for January to consider the wind-down plan, but creditors may have to wait longer to find out how much they will get back.

"I've had nights just sat there in tears, thinking, what is the point," said BD365 Clean's Foskett.

"How much comes in will honestly depend on whether or not the business will still be going at the end of January.

"I don't want to throw the towel in."

SportsTab.title: ATP Finals: Ben Shelton beats Rafael Jodar to move within touching distance of semi-finals
SportsTab.text:
Ben Shelton battled past Rafael Jodar to move within touching distance of a place in the ATP Finals last four.

US Open runner-up Shelton only lost his serve once but still had to fight for just over two hours to beat the fast-rising Spaniard 7-6 (10-8) 7-5.

American Shelton closed out the match with three aces in a row and then wrote "I'll be watching, Arthur" on the camera lens - a reference to the final game in the group.

Shelton will progress to the semi-finals if world number one Alexander Zverev beats France's Arthur Fils later on Thursday.

Fils would need to beat Zverev in straight sets if he is to qualify instead of Shelton.

"I think if he takes Sascha [Zverev] out in straights, I'll say too good and go on holidays," Shelton joked of his good friend Fils.

"I'm always rooting for him [Arthur] and I think he and Sascha will have a great match.

"I'd love to make the semi-finals for the first time. I'll definitely be watching."

Germany's Zverev, unbeaten so far at the season-ending event, is assured of top place in the John McEnroe Group, and will play either Daniil Medvedev or Frances Tiafoe in Saturday's semi-finals.

Shelton did not win a match on his ATP Finals debut last year, but arrived in Turin with a Masters 1000 title and a first Grand Slam final under his belt.

He beat Fils in three entertaining sets in his opening match before being swept aside by Zverev on Tuesday.

Shelton was under pressure against Jodar in the first set, saving two break points and missing a series of routine shots when his opponent was struggling.

However, after taking a tight tie-break, Shelton quickly broke to take control of the third set.

Jodar, competing in his first professional season on the ATP Tour, was strong defensively and wrestled the break back to level at 4-4.

However, he was visibly fatigued and unable to keep Shelton at bay in a series of lengthy rallies, with Shelton breaking for 6-5.

Shelton slipped at the back of court as he served for the match, but recovered quickly to close out victory. He finished with 14 aces to one double fault, having dropped only 11 points behind his first serve.

In the doubles, Britain's Henry Patten and Finnish partner Harri Heliovaara will need to beat French pair Theo Arribage and Albano Olivetti if they are to keep their title defence alive.

Wimbledon champions Patten and Heliovaara have won one and lost one of their three group matches.
