EntertainmentTab.title: Glastonbury 2027 line-up: Harry Styles, Cher, Sam Fender and Billie Eilish to headline
EntertainmentTab.text:
Harry Styles will make his Glastonbury festival debut next year as one of the event's headliners, alongside Sam Fender and Billie Eilish - with Cher among the other stars on the bill.

The veteran US pop icon will play the coveted Sunday afternoon "legends" slot, which is often considered a fourth headline set. It will be her only UK festival appearance of the year.

Other acts on the line-up include Sombr, Sienna Spiro, Lily Allen, The Streets, Chase & Status, Kacey Musgraves, Primal Scream and breakout pop star Adéla.

Tickets for the festival sold out in just 42 minutes last month, with demand particularly high after the event took a year off in 2026.

Electro pioneers Kraftwerk will make their Glastonbury debut with a headline set at West Holts - the festival's third-largest stage.

The event will also welcome experimental Canadian band Angine de Poitrine, who have drawn attention for their prog-rock sound and polka-dotted stage costumes; rap legends De La Soul and Mike D; and pop provocateur FKA Twigs.

"We are so happy to be coming back after our fallow year and, as we head into winter after that peaceful period, we wanted to give you an early musical taster of what's to come at Glastonbury 2027 with this spread of incredible artists," said organiser Emily Eavis.

"We can't wait to see you down here on Worthy Farm in June for some much-needed good times!"

The gates will open at Worthy Farm in Somerset to 200,000 fans on Wednesday 23 June, with music on the main stages kicking off on Friday 25 June.

Tickets prices are at an all-time high of £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket.

Sam Fender will headline the first night, in what will be his second appearance at the festival.

He last played in 2022, immediately before Billie Eilish, and fought back tears as thousands of fans chanted along to hits like Seventeen Going Under and Hypersonic Missiles.

"Me and the boys have never been here before," he said. "We've never been here as punters, never played here before and we're doing that all in one day, which is the most crazy experience."

He will return as one of the UK's biggest rock stars, having won the Mercury Prize for his third album, People Watching, in 2025. Earlier this year, his duet with Olivia Dean - Rein Me In - became the UK's longest-running number one single of all time.

Fender is expected to release a new album ahead of his Glastonbury slot, which will land in the middle of his catchily-titled Proper Massive Stadium Tour.

Harry Styles will take the Pyramid Stage crown on the Saturday.

It comes amid acclaim for his euphoric and athletic Together Together tour, which largely focuses on the understated dance anthems of his fourth album Kiss All The Time. Disco Occasionally.

The pop star has previously been spotted partying at the festival's late-night dance arenas, despite attempting to go incognito in tracksuits and sunglasses.

In 2022, he was rumoured to be making a guest appearance during Eilish's set after his music was played during an early-morning soundcheck - but the duet never materialised.

Instead, Eilish gave a universally well-received performance, described as "imperious [and] hugely engaging" by the Guardian,, external and "proof that the future is here" by the NME, external.

At the time, she was 20 years old - making her the youngest-ever solo act to headline Glastonbury.

Aged between 24 and 32, Styles, Fender and Eilish represent the festival's youngest set of Pyramid Stage headliners since 1997.

Cher, meanwhile, will be the oldest ever act to play the legend slot - strutting through the gates of Worthy Farm at the age of 81.

The diva's appearance will come eight years after her last UK tour, and 63 years into a career that began with her ex-husband Sonny Bono, and recording sessions with Phil Spector's legendary Wrecking Crew band.

She emerged as a solo artist in the 1970s, scoring three US number ones, before switching into disco mode with Take Me Home.

In the 1980s, she became an award-winning actress and scored chart hits with FM rock staples like Turn Back Time and Just Like Jesse James.

Then in 1998, she revitalised her career with club anthem Believe, which helped to popularise the use of autotune in dance music.

Inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2024, she is about to release the second volume of her memoir.

She has previously talked about retiring from live performance - but it seems the lure of Glastonbury was too tempting to turn down.

Cher will follow previous bookings in the crowd-pleasing legends slot including Sir Rod Stewart, Shania Twain, Diana Ross and Kylie Minogue.

More details about the 2027 line-up will be revealed in the New Year. Eavis has previously dismissed rumours that Madonna and Oasis will feature on the bill.

EntertainmentTab.text:
Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.

The Swansea-born actress, 48, told campmates on ITV's I'm a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! that the unnamed male actor had whispered "awful stuff" in her ear before a scene.

"He just spent the whole time just sort of making up this song and chanting about what he was going to do to me, and nobody said anything," she told fellow campmate Mariella Frostrup.

Page has previously described feeling forced to laugh off being groped while filming with a "handsy" TV presenter.

Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show, as fellow celebrities, broadcaster Frostrup and model Leomie Anderson, discussed navigating male-dominated work environments in their careers.

Page said the actor had come up to her "before you were going to do a take or something".

"And it was just, like, really inappropriate, awful stuff."

EntertainmentTab.title: Julio Iglesias faces court investigation over alleged sexual offences
EntertainmentTab.text:
Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members

Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.

The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.

Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations.

But in a statement published on Wednesday, external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.

He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".

Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.

The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.

In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.

The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario, external and television network Univision news, published in January.

In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.

The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.

Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.

The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.

Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.

In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said, external: "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."

On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".

It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".

WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.

But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".

The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.

Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.

He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

EntertainmentTab.title: Hunger Games to show Cardiff teen's artwork before film
EntertainmentTab.text:
A teenage Hunger Games fan has met the cast of the new film after her artwork won a competition, meaning it will be displayed at every cinema screening across the UK.

Freja Brown, 13, won the British Board of Film Classification's (BBFC) create the card competition, which ran ahead of the release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping - the sixth film in the franchise.

Freja, from Cardiff, beat more than 1,000 entries from across the UK and said she was "so grateful" to be chosen.

Her design will be the official BBFC black card, which displays the age rating and classification details of the film before every cinema showing.

The Year nine student, whose favourite subject is art, only started oil painting three years ago.

Her mum Marie recalled the moment Freja found out about the competition while scrolling on social media.

"She just squealed and said, 'there's this competition where you can create a piece of art' and she loves making art. So, she was like, 'I'm gonna do it'."

"She's read all the books and watched all the movies, so being able to combine her love for the Hunger Games with her own art sounded really fun."

Joseph Zada, Mckenna Grace, and Whitney Peak, who play Haymitch, Maysilee, and Lenore Dove in the new film, announced Freja's winning design in a specially recorded video.

Freja said: "I couldn't believe it. I knew that there were lots of other people who had sent in their artwork, so I didn't expect to be chosen and I am so grateful I was."

As part of her prize Freja was also invited to attend a screening of the film in London, where she met some of the stars.

Showing the work to Elle Fanning, who plays Effie Trinket, the actress said: "Oh my God, I thought it was a photo."

Actor Ralph Fiennes said: "It looks wonderful, it's really amazing, I love it."

Speaking of her inspiration, Freja said: "I was inspired by this specific part in the trailer because it shows the Hunger Games arena to be a beautiful place and not the killing machine that it actually is."

Marie, who is a photographer, said her daughter has always been a creative person and "makes stuff all the time", filling their home with her creations.

Marie said her daughter spent more than a month on the piece and worked until the day of the deadline after she "locked in for a whole weekend" to get it done.

She added that she was "so proud" of her daughter.

"It's not just a random piece of art somewhere, it's something that her and her friends get to see, which is fantastic."

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘In our lands the rain is made of bullets’: Palestinian artists look back in anger, melancholy and defiance
EntertainmentTab.text:
In 2006, Simone Fattal painted on to basalt slabs the names of places indelibly associated with massacres in the Levant since 1948: Deir Yassin; Jenin; Qana; Sabra. Through the names, in the same Arabic script, runs a line of poetry by Etel Adnan: “In our lands of drought the rain forever is made of bullets.”

Fattal’s work, which documents atrocities on a material that burst from the earth as lava before settling into stone, introduces a show that likewise combines the recording of history with anger both hot and cold.

The last named of those massacres, perpetrated by a Lebanese Christian phalangist militia during Beirut’s occupation by Israeli forces in 1982, also inspired the poem Praise for the High Shadow by Mahmoud Darwish, a line from which this show takes as its title. Writing in exile in Beirut, Darwish riffed on the sea as a symbol of Palestinian displacement and memory, connecting people dispersed around the eastern Mediterranean to each other and to their homeland. The angry, melancholy, defiant work of these (mostly) Palestinian artists also weaves a traumatic national history into the cosmopolitan culture of the Levant and the interlinked world in which we now live.

It is one lesson of their work that to live in exile is to be waiting. On the floor beside Fattal’s monument stands the suitcase that Hazem Harb carried out of Gaza in 2006; above it are two framed photocollages alluding to the international airport that was bulldozed by the IDF four years earlier. These artefacts beg the question of when, and if, the artist will be able to return to his home, and who will make that decision. That powerlessness and apprehension is etched into the faces of the people photographed by Rula Halawani at Palestinian checkpoints.

Tarek Al-Ghoussein never set foot in his own country. Born in Kuwait to Palestinian parents, he explored his fragmented identity in a troubling series of photographs displayed here on glowing lightboxes. The self in these self-portraits emerges in the unsettling combination of symbols (notably the black-and-white keffiyeh that covers his face) with settings (an airport runway, a target range, an abattoir). A picture of the artist, who died in 2022, looking out to sea like Caspar David Friedrich’s wanderer does not inspire awe at the grandeur of the native landscape so much as indignation at the subject’s separation from his own.

Those who cannot see their own homeland are forced to invent it, which might be why so many storytellers are exiles. Also born in the Gulf to Palestinian émigrés, Basma Al-Sharif set out to tell a conventional “love story” set in the Levant. But she got caught up in the networks of nationalism and identity that must govern her characters’ lives, and so her elaborate fiction instead bears witness – through video, photographs, and botanical drawings of “native” and “invasive” species – to the impossibility of disentangling any individual story from the social and political conditions that frame it. That fact is especially obvious in this charged historical context. It reminds us that to make art for its own sake is a privilege of the few, made possible by injustices that are no less real for being out of sight.

Not only is it a cliche that Palestine is the “land of milk and honey”, as the ironic title of an installation furnished with artificial grass and potted plants suggests, but it is no longer true. At least not in the telling of Khalil Rabah, whose sardonic paintings of road signs indicating bodies of water in parched landscapes offer a reminder that destruction of the natural environment is a strategy of occupation going back at least as far as the Romans (“they make it a desert and call it peace” was Tacitus’s phrase originally). The images of rain, drought, water and sea that recur through the show – and in a neighbouring exhibition of paintings by the Gazan art collective Eltiqa – are not merely poetic metaphors.

For all that this is a show presenting Palestinian histories from Palestinian perspectives, using works from the collection of a UAE-based foundation with a longstanding commitment to that cause, it is only in giving three rooms to the work of Abdul Hay Mosallam Zarara that it slips into agitprop. That these painted reliefs of Palestinian heroes battling imperialist dogs are propaganda does not automatically disqualify them as art – think of John Heartfield’s anti-Nazi photocollages, El Lissitzky’s revolutionary posters, or the vast majority of historical paintings of state leaders and religious icons – but the show would have been better served by a smaller selection, especially if that made space for artists such as Emily Jacir and Mona Hatoum, both of whom are represented in the collection of the Sharjah Art Foundation but surprisingly absent here.

Yet Abdul Hay’s work does serve to connect the Palestinian story to anti-imperialist struggles from Pinochet’s Chile to apartheid-era South Africa. Most notable in the context of this ex-military hospital is a painting commemorating the hunger strikers who died in the Maze in 1981, affirming a link between Irish republicanism and Palestinian independence that endures to this day and informs (and makes possible) such a forthright exhibition in a state-funded institution. Here is a final reminder that art can never entirely be separated from the systems – political, economic, migratory – that produce the societies in which we live, at least until we achieve a collective utopia. Until that time arrives, this timely spotlight on Palestinian artists meets the function ascribed to art by the great critic John Berger, who was born 100 years ago this month: to show the future “what the past has suffered” and thereby to serve as “a meeting place for the invisible, the irreducible, and the enduring”.

EntertainmentTab.title: Alex Cox: ‘John Lydon said Sid and Nancy was a nightmarish piece of garbage’
EntertainmentTab.text:
Looking back, how do you regard your experience with Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas? And did you watch Terry Gilliam’s version? AwapBamBoogers

No, I didn’t watch it. I felt very sad about the whole thing because my wife and I were co-screenwriters. We went out to meet Hunter S Thompson and the poor guy was in a terrible state. He was hoovering up cocaine the whole time we were there. He had a great big TV screen, with a Post-it note saying: “Don’t watch too much TV.” We said we felt like his caseworkers, because all these guys in Hollywood like Johnny Depp were winding him up: “Dr Thompson, do something crazy, go out in the back garden and shoot a can of propane.” That’s all very well, but they were treating him like the freak in the county fairground. How many years was it after Fear and Loathing that the poor guy killed himself? He really needed an intervention. Instead, he was being encouraged by these Hollywood bastards.

The giant boar in Razorback gave me nightmares when I saw it on Moviedrome. Did it give you nightmares too? Sootsayer

I don’t remember. The films in Moviedrome were picked by [producer and director] Nick Freand Jones, who had access to all the films the BBC had under licence and didn’t know what to do with. Some of them I remember really well, but as I’m not so into horror films, I don’t remember Razorback.

What does Liverpool mean to you and how has it influenced your career? AmongstTheWaves

I was born just outside [in Bebington], so I’m not really a scouser. When Liverpool was awarded European capital of culture in 2008, it wasn’t because of the Three Graces on the Pier Head. It was because of the incredible creativity of the people. Liverpool doesn’t really look towards London, it looks across the Atlantic, because of the shipping, so it’s always been very independent. It’s a very interesting city, but, of course, I’m prejudiced.

How did Michael Nesmith from the Monkees help get Repo Man made? Melquiades

We were looking for somebody to executive produce the film and find the money, so I was introduced to him by another producer called Harry Gittes. He liked the script, partially because it had a four-page cartoon at the beginning, and he was very into comic books. Nesmith said to me: “Cox, I don’t think you’re going to have punk rock music all the way through. I want to see a variety of music.” But one song at a time, we put in all these punk songs, and Nesmith went with it. He was a very cool guy.

Do you still agree with the line from Repo Man: “The more you drive, the less intelligent you are?” rewilder

That’s something my wife said when we were still students at UCLA and, at the time, I did believe it. Now I think that if you’re not relying on driver-assist technology, driving is an interesting occupation. It enables you to focus on something in the distance rather than staring at a screen in front of you. Right now I’m crowdfunding Repo Man 2, set in a world of driverless cars. Instead of sneaking down people’s drives, hotwiring cars and running away, the repo man just sits at a computer, takes control and drives the car to the sheriff’s substation or repo yard. It’s a different world, but the same kind of malevolence.

Has crowdfunding become the best way to remain genuinely independent? NorthPixel27

For independent film-makers, yes, because the studios and the big streamers are really only interested in franchises and massive IPs. They want to spend a lot of money, but they don’t really care what the film is. Often they don’t read the script. In the case of Repo Man, it was obvious Universal hadn’t read the script. It got greenlit because of some people Nesmith met in a bar. The people who will back a Kickstarter actually want to see the film.

If you were offered an unlimited budget to make a film on any subject, of any genre, would all that money be a hindrance rather than a help? AD2023

This is irrelevant because I’m never going to be given unlimited funds. But look at people who do have unlimited funds. You look at Christopher Nolan, and how boring his films are. I can’t watch three-hour films unless they’re works of genius. I don’t watch those IP franchise films. Life is too short to waste on rubbish. I mean, what do I care about what some Hollywood nepo baby thinks about Batman? Bond and Le Carré are just propaganda against the Russians. The only really good film that I have seen recently is Flow, this Latvian animated film about what a cat and animals do after all the humans have disappeared. I watched it three times in a row.

Is it a coincidence that both Sid and Nancy and Dogs in Space use going away in a car as a metaphor for death? notvNZ

I haven’t seen Dogs in Space. I think we were trying to find a happy ending, which is impossible for that story. John Lydon was right. I showed him the script and he said: “You should fictionalise this more. You’ve got this wonderful actor, Drew Schofield, playing me in your film. But Drew is a scouser, so he should play it as a Liverpudlian. You should take the film and put it at one remove from the Sex Pistols and it will be more interesting.”

Lydon invited Drew to New York so Drew could study him and learn his ways. When the film came out, he said it was a nightmarish piece of garbage, which was very helpful because it created a controversy. He knew that, because the Sex Pistols were born from controversy.

I watched it again quite recently. It’s a tough film. The ending really is a betrayal because we take the audience into this very dark place, then we release them. If I made it now, I’d have Sid Vicious dying in a pool of blood and vomit.

What are your memories of working with national treasure Kathy Burke? HenleyRegatta

Kathy Burke is fantastic. Everything she says in her book A Mind of My Own is true. She said: “Shane MacGowan used to call me stupid.” I said: “He did that because he was intimidated by you.” MacGowan used to call me “shit for brains”, because he was intimidated by people who were more intelligent than he was.

I was originally asked to direct a video for A Pair of Brown Eyes, one of the Pogues’ early singles. I became friends with the band, so they wrote music for Sid and Nancy and acted in Straight to Hell, which was a wonderful experience. I was also responsible for a terrible thing, because one night we were coming out of the pub, and Shane said to me: “Lend me £10 and I’ll buy you a drink.” I said: “Oh, bugger off,” so he turned his back, walked into the street and got hit by a taxi, and was in hospital for months.

But, going back to the question, Kathy Burke is a person of great intelligence, great sensitivity. It’s been a magnificent honour to have worked with her because I do agree that she’s a national treasure and I love her very much.

What is your favourite murder weapon in movies? Mine’s glue. bisqof

Well, the revolver is always the tidiest, isn’t it? But when we were making Dead Souls, the producer, Merritt Crocker, said: “That’s too easy, because it’s too clean. You should smash his head in with a rock, because then you’re going to be covered in blood and you can’t get away from what you’ve just done.” So I guess the favourite murder weapon depends on the circumstances of the murder.

My eldest daughter is studying media production and aiming to study film production at university. What advice do you have for her? IdoLoveaHat

Make friends with your colleagues and work with them after you leave school. The friends I made at Bristol film school and UCLA, and the students I taught at CU Boulder in Colorado, have become my collaborators. So make friends, collaborate. And when you leave school, stick together and collaborate because you’re much stronger as a group than when you are alone.

Who cares about the Oscars? If I made films, I would try to make them just so that Mark Kermode, Alex Cox and Barry Norman liked them. Grauniad42

No one could be as great as Barry Norman. Surely?

EntertainmentTab.title: Grand Theft Auto would be a huge TV series – here’s why it will never happen
EntertainmentTab.text:
You probably aren’t going to see a Grand Theft Auto TV show anytime soon. Speaking on a recent podcast, Strauss Zelnick, the CEO of the game’s parent company Take-Two Interactive, said that a film or television adaptation of GTA would only happen if its team thought that it would “somehow engage and delight our consumers. It’s a high bar to do that. And, of course, there’s always a risk of failure. So we don’t rule it out, but we’re very, very selective.”

And, well, good. There are a billion reasons why a small screen version would be a terrible idea. Creatively, the thrill of a GTA game is that no two players have the exact same experience. While you might spend your days mowing down civilians and bazookaing police helicopters out of the skies, someone else might take that time to go hiking or explore the waterways. The game is so open-ended, and so moulded to a player’s sensibility, that trying to reduce it to a scripted linear narrative would make it feel uncomfortably thin.

It is also enormous. I am writing this on GTA VI’s launch day, and I am especially sour that I didn’t take the day off to play it. This is because it’s the sort of thing you need to make headway into fast. The main story of the game is 70 hours long, which is like every episode of Game of Thrones ever made dropping at once.

Besides, Take-Two definitely does not need the money. Since its launch in 2013, GTA V is estimated to have made almost $11bn, which is roughly the combined theatrical worldwide gross for every Star Wars film ever made. GTA VI made about $1.6bn in presales alone. If you had full control of the world’s attention like this, you’d be reluctant to risk diluting it with a weak television programme as well.

So it is undoubtedly good news that Grand Theft Auto will only remain a game for ever, joining the ranks of other popular properties that will never make it to screen. Here are its new bedfellows.

Lin-Manuel Miranda has ruled out turning his record-breaking musical into a movie. However, this isn’t because he is married to the sanctity of the live-theatre experience. Instead, he just thinks that his version is as good as it will get. “I have trouble visualising anyone topping what (director) Thomas Kail has done with this live capture,” Miranda told USA Today at a screening of the version currently available on Disney+. “If someone can prove to me that they can top it, I’m open to it. But I haven’t seen it yet.”

In 1992, Art Spiegelman’s Maus became the first graphic novel to ever win a Pulitzer prize. This is for good reason. A memoir about his father who survived Auschwitz, Maus cuts between an account of life in Poland before and during the Holocaust and Art’s visits to his father in New York decades later. Its big conceit is that people are presented as mask-wearing animals. Studios begged to adapt it, but he turned them down. “I like movies, but Maus is better served as a book,” he said in 2022. “[It’s a] more intimate form and comics adhere to the brain better.”

You would imagine that, in a world where a picture book like The Cat in the Hat can be padded out into two different feature-length movies, Bill Watterson’s phone must constantly be ringing. After all, over the years Calvin and Hobbes became home to a vast, rich universe of storytelling. And yet it will never happen. In 2013 Watterson told Mental Floss:“I have zero interest in animating Calvin and Hobbes. If you’ve ever compared a film to a novel it’s based on, you know the novel gets bludgeoned … As a comic strip, Calvin and Hobbes works exactly the way I intended it to. There’s no upside for me in adapting it.”

The pioneering first-person shooter was such a hit on its release in 1998 that Gabe Newell, the co-founder of its studio, Valve, reports receiving endless pitches for film and television adaptations. “And their stories were just so bad,” he told PC Gamer in 2010. “I mean, brutally, the worst. Not understanding what made the game a good game, or what made the property an interesting thing for people to be a fan or enthusiast of.”

GeneralTab.title: Men guilty of abusing Joanne Young, who was drugged and advertised for sex by husband
GeneralTab.text:
Four men have been found guilty of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged and secretly advertised her for sex on the internet, in the first trial of its kind in the UK.

Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife, Joanne Young, over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire.

Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.

Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, beamed at police as she left court wiping her eyes.

On the steps outside the court, Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it".

"The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.

"This has resulted in a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children."

She continued: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to.

"That choice makes them complicit in what was done to me and today's verdicts recognise that."

She said the verdicts were significant "more broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men," sending the message "that you can be believed and understood".

She urged the government to look at the law of consent "as a priority" so that women were "properly protected in the future", adding her abuse case raised "serious questions".

Judge Mr Justice Saini had asked for calm as the verdicts were read out, with Joanne Young sitting in the public gallery surrounded by her family, her hands clasped over her mouth.

She gasped as the first guilty verdicts were read out against Connor Sanderson-Doyle, who dropped his head as he was convicted of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration.

The jury of eight men and four women also convicted Wilkins of one count of assault by penetration.

Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching.

A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February.

The judge commended Joanne Young and said she had shown "amazing bravery through these proceedings".

One police officer could also be seen sobbing as they left the court.

As all defendants were led from the courtroom after being told by the judge to expect lengthy jail terms when they are sentenced on 21 and 22 December, Joanne Young's family could be seen hugging.

Philip Young - who served as a Conservative Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 - drugged and raped his wife over 13 years and invited the men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.

He pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife.

James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, said: "This is the first time in the UK that a jury have convicted or been asked to consider a case of organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse, which has been organised by the husband."

The crimes of the former Tory councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.

Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.

Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.

The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.

Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.

They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".

Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.

A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.

"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.

"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

GeneralTab.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
GeneralTab.text:
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.

Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.

The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.

Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.

He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.

Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.

While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.

Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.

In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.

The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.

It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.

The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.

"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."

Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".

Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".

To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.

Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.

Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.

Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".

He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.

However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.

The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.

Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.

He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".

Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.

Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attaché be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.

He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

GeneralTab.title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'
GeneralTab.text:
Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.

Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.

Here's what you need to know.

The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.

Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.

NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.

In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.

Once established, it was effective.

But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.

Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.

This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.

They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.

When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.

In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.

Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.

Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.

But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.

More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.

The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."

By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.

By contrast, the UK government only requested travellers arriving from high-risk areas to self-isolate for 14 days. The UK government implemented no further border control measures until June 2020.

The report says that border controls were a "critical gap in the UK's ability to limit the spread of the virus" and recommends that in the future "international border control measures should be in place at the earliest stages of a pandemic".

The inquiry report is more positive about the use of smartphone apps, saying digital tools can have a "significant impact on reducing the spread of infection".

It quotes a mathematical modelling study from the US which estimates that, when 75% of people used a contact tracing app in the pandemic, infections were reduced by at least 50%.

Three different apps were developed during Covid - one for England and Wales, another for Scotland and a third for Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.

The inquiry says that took up "valuable time", and it recommends developing a UK-wide digital tool to use in any future outbreak.

It says it is "fundamentally important" that apps and digital tools are as accurate as possible – and people have confidence in them.

In the summer of 2021, as Covid restrictions were relaxed, around 7% of all UK adults were told to self-isolate over a seven-day period, something dubbed by the press as the "pingdemic".

It quotes Treasury estimates suggesting that may have reduced economic growth by as much as 0.3% that month.

GeneralTab.title: Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
GeneralTab.text:
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.

Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.

But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."

The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.

Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is selling shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.

The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.

So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta from StoneX trading.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."

What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.

It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.

"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."

So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.

It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.

With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.

Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.

Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang and another with a company executive who reported to him.

Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.

If Anthropic and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.

While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.

Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.

He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.

That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of new more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.

But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it, the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development, means that buying interest is high.

It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.

With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is to be expected given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.

Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are currently back to $145.

The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.

Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.

"Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."

Fiona Cincotta believes Anthropic's IPO is about far more than just Anthropic. "I think what's going to be really interesting here is I think it can actually be used as a valuation benchmark for the entire AI ecosystem," she says.

"That's why I don't think this is just going to affect the share price of Anthropic. I think this is going to have much wider implications across the whole AI trade."

Two things can be true at the same time. The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful - FOMO is a powerful emotion in financial markets. But its probable success won't soothe the unease in some quarters that not every company, every investor and every citizen will think of AI as the answer to humanity's problems.

GeneralTab.title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
GeneralTab.text:
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.

Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.

McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."

The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.

Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.

McDonald's workers speak out over sexual abuse claims

McDonald's boss on abuse claims: 'I don't want to talk about the past'

Every McDonald's warned over staff sexual abuse

Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.

She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.

"I got the hell out of there," she says.

Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.

Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".

Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.

"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.

"And why would you? That is literally a child still."

Hundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.

The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.

The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.

Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.

Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees".

"It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it a lot safer, I think, as well. And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''

She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out.

"And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"

articles.title: Men guilty of abusing Joanne Young, who was drugged and advertised for sex by husband
articles.text:
Four men have been found guilty of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged and secretly advertised her for sex on the internet, in the first trial of its kind in the UK.

Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife, Joanne Young, over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire.

Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.

Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, beamed at police as she left court wiping her eyes.

On the steps outside the court, Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it".

"The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.

"This has resulted in a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children."

She continued: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to.

"That choice makes them complicit in what was done to me and today's verdicts recognise that."

She said the verdicts were significant "more broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men," sending the message "that you can be believed and understood".

She urged the government to look at the law of consent "as a priority" so that women were "properly protected in the future", adding her abuse case raised "serious questions".

Judge Mr Justice Saini had asked for calm as the verdicts were read out, with Joanne Young sitting in the public gallery surrounded by her family, her hands clasped over her mouth.

She gasped as the first guilty verdicts were read out against Connor Sanderson-Doyle, who dropped his head as he was convicted of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration.

The jury of eight men and four women also convicted Wilkins of one count of assault by penetration.

Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching.

A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February.

The judge commended Joanne Young and said she had shown "amazing bravery through these proceedings".

One police officer could also be seen sobbing as they left the court.

As all defendants were led from the courtroom after being told by the judge to expect lengthy jail terms when they are sentenced on 21 and 22 December, Joanne Young's family could be seen hugging.

Philip Young - who served as a Conservative Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 - drugged and raped his wife over 13 years and invited the men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.

He pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife.

James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, said: "This is the first time in the UK that a jury have convicted or been asked to consider a case of organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse, which has been organised by the husband."

The crimes of the former Tory councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.

Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.

Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.

The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.

Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.

They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".

Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.

A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.

"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.

"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

articles.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
articles.text:
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.

Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.

The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.

Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.

He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.

Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.

While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.

Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.

In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.

The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.

It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.

The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.

"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."

Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".

Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".

To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.

Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.

Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.

Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".

He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.

However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.

The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.

Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.

He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".

Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.

Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attaché be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.

He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

articles.title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'
articles.text:
Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.

Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.

Here's what you need to know.

The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.

Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.

NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.

In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.

Once established, it was effective.

But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.

Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.

This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.

They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.

When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.

In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.

Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.

Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.

But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.

More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.

The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."

By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.

By contrast, the UK government only requested travellers arriving from high-risk areas to self-isolate for 14 days. The UK government implemented no further border control measures until June 2020.

The report says that border controls were a "critical gap in the UK's ability to limit the spread of the virus" and recommends that in the future "international border control measures should be in place at the earliest stages of a pandemic".

The inquiry report is more positive about the use of smartphone apps, saying digital tools can have a "significant impact on reducing the spread of infection".

It quotes a mathematical modelling study from the US which estimates that, when 75% of people used a contact tracing app in the pandemic, infections were reduced by at least 50%.

Three different apps were developed during Covid - one for England and Wales, another for Scotland and a third for Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.

The inquiry says that took up "valuable time", and it recommends developing a UK-wide digital tool to use in any future outbreak.

It says it is "fundamentally important" that apps and digital tools are as accurate as possible – and people have confidence in them.

In the summer of 2021, as Covid restrictions were relaxed, around 7% of all UK adults were told to self-isolate over a seven-day period, something dubbed by the press as the "pingdemic".

It quotes Treasury estimates suggesting that may have reduced economic growth by as much as 0.3% that month.
